objective: Recognizing an allergic reaction and responding to it
secondaryObjectives: Know that epinephrine is the first drug in anaphylaxis, and ask an alert client to report any change in breathing afterwards
Unexpected response to therapy, and recognizing complications early
Organize and prioritize care by client need, using airway, breathing and circulation and Maslow's hierarchy to decide what comes first
Client allergies: collecting the data and acting on it
Reporting adverse effects to the registered nurse or provider

brief.situation: 10:12 on a subacute rehabilitation unit. You are the LPN. At 10:00 you gave Mrs. Brewer, 72, the first dose of oral amoxicillin newly ordered for a urinary infection. Her call light is on; she is sitting in her chair and says her skin is itchy and her throat feels 'tight'.
handover: She is 9 days after a hip replacement, walks with a walker and a standby assist, about 70 kg.

Unit anaphylaxis standing order: epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg IM to the outer thigh for suspected anaphylaxis, repeat once after 5 minutes if not improving; call 911; oxygen; notify the RN supervisor and the provider.
The electronic record lists 'no known allergies'.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
She is changing minute by minute. Some steps take a minute or more.
Partway through you are asked to write what is happening and why. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Untreated, she reaches shock and airway obstruction in about 12 minutes. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

effects.log: She says: "Penicillin gave me a rash as a girl, I told them when I came in." The scanned admission form lists 'penicillin (rash)'; the electronic record does not. Amoxicillin is a penicillin.

epi.label: Epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg IM to the outer thigh (standing order)

why.question: What is happening, why, and what do you do in what order? What must you not do?

parts.label: Recognition
parts.criteria: Names anaphylaxis: skin (hives, lip swelling) with airway or breathing signs (tight throat, hoarse voice, wheeze) and falling BP minutes after a first dose of a penicillin; finds the penicillin allergy missing from the electronic record.
parts.modelAnswer: Anaphylaxis: hives and lip swelling plus a tight throat, hoarse voice and wheeze, with her BP dropping, 12 minutes after her first amoxicillin. Her old penicillin allergy is on the paper admission form but not in the electronic record.

parts.label: Priorities
parts.criteria: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM to the thigh first under the standing order; call 911 and the RN; keep her lying with legs raised, or semi-sitting if breathing is easier, and never stand or walk her; oxygen; a second dose after 5 minutes if not improving; antihistamine is not the first drug; record the reaction and the allergy, and report the missed allergy.
parts.modelAnswer: Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM to the outer thigh now, then 911 and the RN supervisor. Keep her down: lying with legs raised, or semi-sitting if that helps her breathe; no standing, no walk to the bathroom. Oxygen. If she isn't better in 5 minutes, the second dose. The diphenhydramine can wait; it does nothing for her airway or blood pressure. Then record it all, add the allergy to her record and report how it was missed.

noProgress.rationale: Anaphylaxis still unhandled to emergency care 45 minutes in has gone without the escalation the standing order requires, so this case calls it harm.

expertPath.text: Look and listen: hives, puffy lips, hoarse voice, wheeze, 12 minutes after a first penicillin. Anaphylaxis.
Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM to the outer thigh. 911. RN supervisor to the room. Recline her with legs up; oxygen; vital signs machine on.
Not improving: second dose. Ask about allergies: penicillin rash, on paper, not in the record.
Paramedics take over. Record the reaction, add the allergy, report the missed allergy.

collapse.headline: She collapsed
collapse.body: Epinephrine first and keep her down. Standing someone in anaphylaxis can drop the blood pressure past the point of no pulse.

handedOver.headline: Anaphylaxis treated and handed over
handedOver.body: You recognized anaphylaxis, gave epinephrine first under the standing order, called 911, kept her down and found the missed allergy. That is the expert path.

handedOverLate.headline: Handed over, by a slower or riskier route
handedOverLate.body: Check when the first epinephrine went in, whether an antihistamine came first, when 911 was called, and how she was positioned.

time_up.headline: No emergency care
time_up.body: Anaphylaxis is an emergency: epinephrine, 911, keep the person down.

scoring.modelReasoning: Hives and lip swelling with a tight throat, hoarse voice and wheeze minutes after a first dose of a penicillin is anaphylaxis. Epinephrine IM to the outer thigh is the first drug, given at once under the standing order and repeated after 5 minutes if she is not improving; 911 and the RN supervisor are called at the same time. Keep her lying with legs raised, or semi-sitting if that eases her breathing, and avoid sudden changes in posture: standing or walking can make her collapse. Oxygen helps; antihistamines do not treat the airway or blood pressure and never come first. Afterwards record the reaction, add the penicillin allergy that was on her paper admission form but missing from the electronic record, and report the gap.

emsQ.ask: While the paramedics come, she asks to use the bathroom. What do you do?

choices.label: Bedpan where she is; she stays down
Walk her there with the walker
Stand her briefly to check her legs

emsQ.explain: Avoid sudden changes in posture in anaphylaxis: keep her lying or semi-sitting until she is stable and handed over.
